full_text_en:
Zheng Yali v. Seiko Epson Corporation, Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office, Foshan Kaideli Office Supplies Co., Ltd., and Shenzhen Yicai Industrial Development Co., Ltd. — administrative dispute over patent invalidation

【Ruling Summary】

The "scope of the original description and claims" as referred to in Article 33 of the Patent Law shall include the content explicitly expressed in words or graphics in the original description, its drawings, and the claims, as well as the content that can be directly and clearly derived by a person of ordinary skill in the art through a comprehensive review of the original description, its drawings, and the claims. As long as the derived content is obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art, it may be determined that such content falls within the scope of the original description and claims; compared with the above content, if the amended patent application documents do not introduce new technical content, it may be determined that the amendment to the patent application documents does not exceed the scope of the original description and claims.

There is both a certain connection and a clear difference between the restrictions on amendment of patent application documents and the scope of patent protection. During the examination of a request for invalidation, when the patentee of an invention or utility model patent amends its claims, it shall be limited by the scope of protection of the original patent and shall not expand the scope of protection of the original patent. When an invention patent applicant makes an active amendment at the time of filing a request for substantive examination or within three months from the date of receipt of the notice issued by the patent administration department of the State Council informing that the invention patent application has entered the substantive examination stage, it may either expand or narrow the scope of protection claimed in the original claims, provided that the amendment does not exceed the scope of the original description and claims.

The doctrine of estoppel shall be applicable in the patent grant and validity confirmation procedures, but it is subject to the limitations of its own conditions for application as well as the limitations of other related principles and legal provisions. In the patent grant procedure, the relevant laws have already granted the applicant the right to amend the patent application documents. As long as such amendments do not exceed the scope of the original description and claims, the doctrine of estoppel should have no room for application within the scope of such amendments.

Administrative Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

Applicant for Retrial Zheng Yali, in connection with the administrative dispute over patent invalidation with Seiko Epson Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Seiko Epson), the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board), Foshan Kaideli Office Supplies Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Kaideli Company), and Shenzhen Yicai Industrial Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yicai Company), being dissatisfied with the administrative judgment (2009) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 327 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court of the People's Republic of China, applied to this Court for retrial. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel to review the case and has now concluded the review.

Seiko Epson, being dissatisfied with the Invalidation Request Decision No. 11291 (hereinafter referred to as Decision No. 11291) of the Patent Reexamination Board, filed a lawsuit within the statutory period before the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court of the People's Republic of China, claiming that Decision No. 11291 had serious errors in the examination procedure and factual findings, and requested the court to revoke it in accordance with law. The main reasons were: 1. Decision No. 11291 violated proper procedures. 2. The relevant findings in Decision No. 11291 deviated from objective facts. When responding to the first Office Action in the substantive examination stage, the plaintiff had already interpreted "storage device" as "the semiconductor storage device 61 shown in (b) of Figure 7", and interpreted "memory device" as "the circuit board described in the specification and drawings and the semiconductor storage device provided thereon". 3. The interpretation of "storage device" in Decision No. 11291 contradicted the interpretation standards for functional limitation features in relevant precedents of the Beijing High People's Court. 4. The relevant additional technical features in dependent claims 4 and 34, as well as the technical solution of claim 8, did not exceed the scope disclosed in the original specification.

The Patent Reexamination Board responded: 1. Regarding the examination procedure. The examination procedure in this case complied with the provisions of Section 4.5, Chapter 3, Part IV of the Patent Examination Guidelines concerning the consolidation of cases for trial. 2. Regarding Article 33 of the Patent Law (as amended in 2000) (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Law). (1) The "scope of the original description and claims" should be taken as the basis for determining whether the applicant's amendment complies with Article 33 of the Patent Law, and the applicant's interpretation of the claims in the statement of opinions cannot be used as a basis for determining facts; (2) Section 3.2.1, Chapter 2, Part II of the Patent Examination Guidelines clearly stipulates that "for technical features defined by functional limitations contained in the claims, they shall be understood as covering all implementation manners that can achieve the said function"; (3) Regarding specific opinions on the relevant claims, the Board insists on the opinions in the decision. In summary, Decision No. 11291 has clear factual findings, correct application of laws and regulations, and lawful examination procedures, and the court is requested to uphold the decision.

The Beijing First Intermediate People's Court found at first instance: The patent at issue in Decision No. 11291 is the invention patent No. 00131800.4 entitled "Ink Cartridge" (hereinafter referred to as the patent-in-suit), whose grant was announced by the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China on June 23, 2004. The patent-in-suit is a divisional application of invention patent application No. 99800780.3, with a filing date of May 18, 1999, and the earliest priority date of May 18, 1998, and the patentee is Seiko Epson. The claims as granted and announced in the patent-in-suit include 42 claims.

The Patent Reexamination Board held an oral hearing on April 27, 2006, regarding the above request for invalidation.

With respect to the patent-in-suit, Zheng Yali filed a request for invalidation with the Patent Reexamination Board on June 15, 2007, on the grounds that the patent-in-suit did not comply with the provisions of Article 33 and Article 26, paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, and requested that the patent-in-suit be declared completely invalid, and submitted the published specification of the original divisional application No. 99800780.3 as evidence. On July 3, 2007, Zheng Yali submitted a statement of opinions to the Patent Reexamination Board, arguing that the granted claims of the patent-in-suit also lacked novelty and inventive step as required by Article 22, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the Patent Law, and submitted relevant evidence at the same time.

With respect to the patent-in-suit, Yicai Company filed a request for invalidation with the Patent Reexamination Board on October 31, 2007, based on the exact same grounds and evidence as Kaideli Company.

In response to the above requests for invalidation, Seiko Epson submitted a statement of opinions and a replacement page of amended claims on September 18, 2007. The amended claims were identical in content to the claims submitted on March 1, 2006. In response to Zheng Yali's request for invalidation, Seiko Epson also submitted the statement of opinions submitted when responding to the first Office Action during the substantive examination stage of the patent-in-suit, to prove that the amendments made during the substantive examination stage did not exceed the scope of the original disclosure and complied with Article 33 of the Patent Law.

On March 25, 2008, the Patent Reexamination Board held an oral hearing.

The Patent Reexamination Board held that: 1. This patent is a divisional application of invention patent application No. 99800780.3, which itself is an international application (PCT/JP99/02579) entering the Chinese national phase, meaning the application documents of invention patent application No. 99800780.3 are equivalent to the Chinese translation of international application PCT/JP99/02579. The terms "storage device" in claims 1 and 40, and "memory device" in claims 8, 12, and 29 of this patent were all amended during the substantive examination stage. The PCT/JP99/02579 international application documents filed on the filing date and the specification and claims of invention patent application No. 99800780.3 contained no written record of "storage device" or "memory device," but only "semiconductor storage device." A "storage device" is a device for storing information data, which includes various types such as magnetic bubble storage devices, ferroelectric storage devices, etc., in addition to semiconductor storage devices. The original specification and claims of this patent were directed to a semiconductor storage device and did not involve other types of storage devices, nor could it be directly and unambiguously derived that the ink cartridge was equipped with other types of storage devices. Therefore, a person skilled in the art could not directly and unambiguously determine "storage device" from the "semiconductor storage device" recorded in the original specification and claims. Similarly, "memory device" could not be directly and unambiguously determined from the "semiconductor storage device" recorded in the original specification and claims, causing independent claims 1, 8, 12, 29, and 40 and their respective dependent claims to fail to comply with the provisions of Article 33 of the Patent Law. The original specification's statements, "This is because the printing device must be brought to the manufacturer, and the storage device recording control data must be replaced" and "wherein a semiconductor storage device and an electrode connected to the storage device are provided on an ink cartridge," were both recorded in the background art section. Moreover, the statement "This is because the printing device must be brought to the manufacturer, and the storage device recording control data must be replaced" was directed to printing devices in the prior art, and "storage device" in "wherein a semiconductor storage device and an electrode connected to the storage device are provided on an ink cartridge" should be an abbreviation for "semiconductor storage device" and does not refer to a different technical feature. This patent is an improvement directed to an ink cartridge equipped with a semiconductor storage device, specifically targeting the "semiconductor storage device," not "storage device" or storage devices other than "semiconductor storage devices." The term "memory device" itself does not carry the meaning of a combination of "semiconductor storage device" and "circuit board." Furthermore, based on the limitations placed on "memory device" by claims 13 and 14 of this patent, "memory device" is not, as Seiko Epson claimed, a "combination of a 'semiconductor storage device' and a 'circuit board'." 2. The additional technical feature of dependent claim 4, "the width of the second wall is narrower than other walls of the housing," and the additional technical feature of dependent claim 34, "the width of the side wall is narrower than other side walls of the housing," were neither recorded in the original specification and claims, nor could they be directly and unambiguously determined from the original specification and claims, thus exceeding the scope of the original specification and claims. 3. The overall technical solution of claim 8 of this patent, which includes the technical feature "the contact row closest to the ink supply port is longer than the contact row farthest from the ink supply port," was also not recorded in the original specification and claims. The embodiments shown in Figures 6 and 7 are directed to an ink cartridge where the circuit board is arranged on a side wall perpendicular to the bottom wall where the ink supply port is located, while claim 8 of this patent also includes situations such as an ink cartridge where the circuit board, contacts, and ink supply port are located on the same wall, which were not recorded in the original specification and claims and could not be directly and unambiguously determined from the original specification and claims. Therefore, the amendment to claim 8 of this patent also exceeded the scope of the original specification and claims. 4. In view of the fact that this patent has already failed to comply with the provisions of Article 33 of the Patent Law, the other invalidation grounds and evidence are no longer evaluated. Accordingly, on April 15, 2008, the Patent Reexamination Board issued Decision No. 11291, declaring all claims of this patent invalid.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held at first instance: 1. Regarding whether the amendments to claims 1, 8, 12, 29, and 40 of this patent complied with Article 33 of the Patent Law. The terms "storage device" and "memory device" as amended in the claims of this patent are clear terms. A person skilled in the art knows that "storage device" is not limited to "semiconductor storage device," and "memory device" is not equivalent to "circuit board and semiconductor storage device provided thereon." By amending "semiconductor storage device" to "storage device" during the substantive examination stage, the patent applicant expanded the scope of protection to all types of storage devices. "Memory device" was not recorded in the original specification and claims, and a person skilled in the art could not directly and unambiguously determine from the original specification and claims that "memory device" refers to "circuit board and semiconductor storage device provided thereon." Accordingly, the determination in Decision No. 11291 that claims 1, 8, 12, 29, and 40 of this patent did not comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law was not improper. 2. Regarding whether the amendments to claims 4, 8, and 34 of this patent complied with Article 33 of the Patent Law. For claims 4 and 34 of this patent, Figures 6 and 26 of the drawings could not directly and unambiguously determine that the side wall on which the circuit board and semiconductor storage device are arranged is narrower than the other walls. For claim 8 of this patent, the explanation provided in the statement of opinion cannot be used as a basis to limit the claim under the law, and Figures 6 and 7 only reflect the situation where the circuit board, contacts, and ink supply port are located on different walls, but do not reflect an ink cartridge where the circuit board, contacts, and ink supply port are located on the same wall, nor can the arrangement of the lengths of the contact rows in such an ink cartridge structure be directly and unambiguously determined. Accordingly, the determination in Decision No. 11291 that claims 4, 8, and 34 did not comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law was not improper. Pursuant to Article 54(1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, on December 20, 2008, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered Administrative Judgment (2008) Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 1030: upholding Decision No. 11291 of the Patent Reexamination Board. The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 was borne by Seiko Epson.

Seiko Epson, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court, claiming: 1. According to the universally recognized "prosecution history estoppel" principle in the interpretation of patent claims, the meaning of the technical terms in this case should be determined based on the interpretation given by the appellant during the substantive examination stage to obtain the patent, i.e., "storage device" should be interpreted as "'semiconductor storage device 61' as shown in Figure 7(b)," and "memory device" should be interpreted as "referring to the circuit board recorded in the specification and drawings and the semiconductor storage device provided thereon." 2. In Decision No. 11291, the interpretation of "storage device" contradicts the interpretation standards for functional limitation features in relevant precedents of the Beijing High People's Court. 3. The relevant additional technical features in dependent claims 4 and 34 were reflected in the original specification's drawings, Figure 6(a), Figure 26, etc., and did not exceed the scope of the original disclosure. For the technical solution of claim 8, the appellant also provided an explanation when responding to the first office action. Therefore, this patent complies with Article 33 of the Patent Law. The Patent Reexamination Board, Kaide Li Company, Zheng Yali, and Yicai Company abided by the first-instance judgment.

The Beijing High People's Court found that the facts ascertained were consistent with those of the first-instance court. Additionally, it found: On November 8, 2002, the State Intellectual Property Office issued a first office action regarding this patent application. In response to this office action, on May 9, 2003, Seiko Epson submitted a statement of opinion, amending the original claims, changing the original claim 23 to the new claim 1. Addressing the examiner's issue of "amendment exceeding scope," Seiko Epson stated in paragraph 2.2 of the statement of opinion: "Claim 23 relates to Figures 6 and 7. The applicant explains that 'storage device' refers to 'semiconductor storage device 61' as shown in Figure 7(b)"; in paragraph 3.1 of the statement of opinion, it stated: "The applicant first wishes to explain that the 'memory device' mentioned in this claim and subsequent claims refers to the circuit board recorded in the specification and drawings and the semiconductor storage device provided thereon."

The Beijing High People's Court held that the standard for determining whether an amendment exceeds the scope is whether the amendment "exceeds the scope of the original specification and claims" and whether it "exceeds the scope disclosed in the original application," i.e., whether a person of ordinary skill in the art, after reading the original specification and claims, can unambiguously determine the amended content from the records of those documents. When determining whether an amendment exceeds the scope, attention must also be paid to whether the amended technical solution constitutes a new technical solution. Furthermore, the applicant's statements during the patent grant process may serve as a reference for whether the amendment exceeds the scope, but such statements cannot be the sole basis for determination.

(I) Regarding whether the amendment of "storage device" in claims 1 and 40 of this patent violated Article 33 of the Patent Law

The understanding of technical terms and features should be made from the perspective of a person skilled in the art, considering the specific context in which the technical term or feature is used. In this case, the terms "storage device" in claims 1 and 40 and "memory device" in claims 8, 12, and 29 of this patent were all amended during the substantive examination stage. The original disclosure of this patent contained records of "semiconductor storage device" and "storage device" in the relevant claims. The original specification of this patent had already stated that the technical problem solved by this patent was that "the printing device must be brought to the manufacturer, and the storage device recording control data must be replaced," and the background art also recorded "wherein a semiconductor storage device and an electrode connected to the storage device are provided on an ink cartridge." Furthermore, other parts of the original specification all used "semiconductor storage device." A person skilled in the art, by reading the original claims and specification, could unambiguously determine that the patent applicant used "storage device" in the sense of "semiconductor storage device" in the specification. Moreover, whether before or after the amendment, "storage device" was actually used in the sense of "semiconductor storage device," and did not create a new technical solution, nor would a person skilled in the art understand it as such. In the statement of opinion submitted by the patentee in response to the office action during the substantive examination stage, a clear limitation was made for "storage device." Specifically, for "storage device," the statement of opinion recorded, "The applicant explains that 'storage device' refers to 'semiconductor storage device 61' as shown in Figure 7(b)," and the penultimate paragraph on page 1 of the original specification recorded, "wherein a semiconductor storage device and an electrode connected to the storage device are provided on an ink cartridge," indicating that "storage device" is an abbreviation for "semiconductor storage device."

The entity for determining whether an amendment exceeds the scope is a person skilled in the art, who is an ordinary technician with professional knowledge in the relevant field and capable of understanding the technical content in that field. Although "storage device" has a general meaning that includes not only semiconductor storage devices but also various types such as magnetic bubble storage devices and ferroelectric storage devices, in the specific field of printer ink cartridges to which this patent belongs, given that the background art has clearly indicated that the reference is to a "semiconductor storage device," a person skilled in the art would not understand it as the broader concept of "storage device." The first-instance judgment and Decision No. 11291 erred in their understanding of "storage device," which is hereby corrected. Seiko Epson's appeal claim that the amendment of "storage device" complied with Article 33 of the Patent Law has factual and legal basis and should be supported. The Patent Reexamination Board shall reissue an examination decision on this matter.

(II) Regarding whether the amendment of "memory device" in claims 8, 12, and 29 of this patent violated Article 33 of the Patent Law

The amendment of "memory device" in this patent, although also made during the substantive examination stage, is different from the amendment of "storage device." The original claims and specification of this patent never contained a record of "memory device"; this term was newly added by the patent applicant. Newly added content that was not recorded does not comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law. Furthermore, although the patent applicant made a clear limitation for "memory device" in the statement of opinion responding to the office action during the substantive examination stage, as determined above, a mere explanation in a statement of opinion cannot serve as a basis for allowing the amendment. Accordingly, the first-instance judgment and Decision No. 11291 correctly determined that "memory device" was not recorded in the original specification and claims, and a person skilled in the art could not clearly determine from the original specification and claims that "memory device" is "a circuit board and a semiconductor storage device provided thereon." Seiko Epson's appeal claim that the amendment of "memory device" complied with Article 33 of the Patent Law cannot be established and is hereby rejected.

Given that claims 8, 12, and 29 of this patent are determined not to comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law, and the dependent claims of the above claims also fail to overcome this defect, claims 8, 12, and 29 of this patent and their respective dependent claims all do not comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law. The determination in Decision No. 11291 of the Patent Reexamination Board that claims 8, 12, and 29 of this patent all do not comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law is correct and shall be upheld.

(III) Regarding whether the feature in claim 4 of this patent, "the width of the second wall is narrower than other walls of the housing," complies with Article 33 of the Patent Law

The feature "the width of the second wall is narrower than other walls of the housing" in claim 4 of this patent was neither recorded in the original claims and specification, nor could it be unambiguously derived from the original claims and specification, and thus does not comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law. The drawings of the specification are used to represent the shape, structure, and positional relationship of the product. For other technical fields, the drawings of the specification may be circuit diagrams, chemical structural formulas, or flowcharts of reaction method processes. In this case, the drawings of the specification of this patent are not standard mechanical drawings; they merely reflect the structure and positional relationship of the technical solution of this patent. The drawings cannot unambiguously determine that "the width of the second wall is narrower than other walls of the housing." The determination in Decision No. 11291 of the Patent Reexamination Board that claim 4 of this patent does not comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law is correct. Seiko Epson's appeal claim that Figure 6 of the specification of this patent could reflect the technical feature "the width of the second wall is narrower than other walls of the housing" in claim 4 of this patent, and thus complies with Article 33 of the Patent Law, cannot be established.

Zheng Yali, dissatisfied with the above judgment of second instance, petitioned this Court for retrial on the grounds that the judgment of second instance was unclear in the finding of facts and erroneous in the application of law, and requested that the judgment of second instance be revoked according to law and the judgment of first instance be upheld. The main reasons were: 1. The judgment of second instance was erroneous in finding that the term "storage device" was used in the sense of "semiconductor storage device" in the original publication (Patent Application Publication No. 99800780.3 for invention). The 75 claims in the original publication did not mention a "storage device" on the ink cartridge. The term "storage device" appeared twice in the description at lines 24-27 on page 1, both in the section introducing the prior art. The first "storage device" (line 24, page 1 of the description) should refer to a storage device on the printing apparatus, without specifying what kind of storage device, and had no connection to the "semiconductor storage device" installed on the ink cartridge in this patent. The second "storage device" (line 27, page 1 of the description) could be understood as an abbreviation for the "semiconductor storage device" in line 26 of page 1 of the description. This was a case of first using the full name then the abbreviation within one sentence. Such an abbreviation could only apply within that sentence and could not be extended beyond it. 2. The amendments to this patent should be invalidated because they expanded the scope of protection, and the judgment of second instance erred in narrowly interpreting the scope of protection of this patent. (1) The judgment of second instance erred in applying Article 56 of the Patent Law. That provision, stating that "the scope of protection of the invention or utility model patent shall be determined by the content of the claims," not only indicated that the content of the claims constitutes the scope of patent protection but also informed the applicant to select and clearly write the content for which protection is sought into the claims. Another implication of "shall be determined by" is that if there is a conflict between the concept in the claims and the corresponding concept in the specification, the content of the concept in the claims shall prevail. Since different understandings of the connotation and denotation of each term in the claims could change the overall scope of protection, the concept in the claims must be given priority to reflect "shall be determined by." The provision that "the description and drawings may be used to interpret the claims" means that the description and drawings serve only as examples and explanations to facilitate understanding of the solution in the claims. The concept of "storage device" in independent claims 1 and 40 of this patent was clear without need for interpretation and encompassed storage devices of various types, including optical, magnetic, electrical, and semiconductor types, as a superordinate concept. The condition for interpreting such a clear superordinate concept as a specific subordinate concept was that the specification must provide a clear definition designating it as a semiconductor storage device. In the absence of a clear definition in the specification, interpreting it as a superordinate concept was correct and a lawful way to maintain the seriousness of the claims. The judgment of second instance interpreted the clear term in the specification as being the same as the superordinate concept in the claims, violating Article 56 of the Patent Law. (2) In administrative disputes concerning patent invalidation, the meaning of claim concepts cannot be interpreted using the applicant's statements made during the patent grant and confirmation proceedings. The granted patent text is made public, but statements made during patent examination do not appear in the published text. After the public receives the information from the granted patent text, the scope of the claims as published affects their subsequent actions. The public's understanding of the claims is based on the literal meaning of the words in the claims. If the true meaning of these words requires reference to statements that the public cannot see, it would be unfair to the public and could lead to serious problems of the specification misleading the public. Therefore, it was improper to interpret clear concepts in the claims of the granted publication using the content of statements made during patent examination.

Seiko Epson responded, arguing that the judgment of second instance correctly found that the technical feature of "storage device" in independent claims 1 and 40 and their dependent claims did not exceed the scope of the original disclosure, which was consistent with the facts and law. The petitioner's grounds for retrial lacked factual and legal basis and should be rejected. The main reasons were: 1. The term "storage device" in the granted patent of this patent should be interpreted as a semiconductor storage device. The term "storage device" as used in claim 2 of the original publication and in the prior art section of the description was an abbreviation for semiconductor storage device. Based on the principle that the same term in the same patent should have the same meaning, "storage device" in this patent should refer only to a semiconductor storage device. A person of ordinary skill in the art, considering the technical problem to be solved and the purpose of the invention, could also unambiguously understand "storage device" in the claims as a semiconductor storage device. According to the patent examination file of this patent, "storage device" in the claims should also be determined to refer to a semiconductor storage device. Decision No. 11291, by interpreting the "storage device" in the claims literally as various storage devices with information data storage functions, did not reflect the objective facts of this patent and violated the correct claim interpretation methodology. 2. The standard for interpreting claims in patent infringement proceedings should be consistent with that in patent confirmation proceedings. Based on the principle of certainty of patent rights, for the same patent right, whether in infringement or confirmation proceedings, the interpretation standard for its claims should be uniform to maintain consistency in its scope of protection. If different interpretation standards were applied in infringement and confirmation proceedings, leading to different scopes of protection for the same patent right, it would cause unfair legal consequences to the public or the patentee. 3. The patent examination file should serve as a basis for interpreting "storage device" in claims 1 and 40 of this patent. (1) According to Article 3 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Patent Infringement Dispute Cases, the patent examination file can be used as a basis for interpreting claims, having the same interpretative effect as the description, drawings, and relevant claims in the claim set, and has priority over "reference books, textbooks, and common knowledge documents as well as the ordinary understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art." In this case, for the term "storage device," not only did the background art section of the original description and original claim 2 use the term in the sense of "semiconductor storage device," but the patent examination file also clearly limited the technical meaning of this term in this patent to "semiconductor storage device." Under these circumstances, "storage device" should be interpreted as "semiconductor storage device." Since the meaning of the technical feature "storage device" in the claims could be clearly determined using the patent examination file, it was not necessary to further interpret the term "storage device" literally by reference to reference books, textbooks, common knowledge documents, or the ordinary understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art. Decision No. 11291 violated the order of priority of interpretation bases and should be corrected according to law. (2) Since the limiting interpretation of "storage device" in the patent examination file had binding force for interpreting claims in patent infringement proceedings, excluding the interpretative role of the patent examination file in the patent confirmation proceedings of this case would be extremely unfair to the patentee. If infringement proceedings involving this patent occurred, in that proceeding, when interpreting "storage device" in the claims, whether according to the aforementioned Article 3 of the Judicial Interpretation on claim interpretation bases or Article 6 on estoppel, the people's court would interpret the technical meaning of "storage device" in this patent as "semiconductor storage device." In patent infringement proceedings, Epson could not interpret storage devices other than semiconductor storage devices into the scope of protection of this patent. In other words, this patent could not protect ink cartridges using other storage devices in infringement proceedings. Therefore, if the opposite claim interpretation method was adopted in the confirmation proceedings of this case, interpreting it as various storage devices including semiconductor storage devices, and thereby finding that the amendments exceeded the scope of the original disclosure and declaring the patent completely invalid, this would essentially force technical solutions that could not obtain protection in infringement proceedings into the scope of protection of this patent. Such a practice and its result were manifestly unfair to the patentee. (3) The weaker public notice function of the patent examination file compared to the claims and specification could not be used to deny its interpretative effect on the claims. The patent examination file was also open to the public and had a public notice function. Therefore, since the relevant judicial interpretation had clearly listed it as a basis for claim interpretation, its interpretative effect could not be denied based on the strength of its public notice function. (4) A limiting interpretation made by a patent applicant through an amendment voluntarily made to the claims was binding on determining the scope of protection of those claims, and the scope of protection should be determined based on that limiting interpretation. In this case, although Seiko Epson's amendment to the technical feature "storage device" during substantive examination was voluntary, the limiting interpretation in the patent examination file regarding this voluntary amendment was accepted by the examiner and became the basis for granting this patent. It was not appropriate to deny the legal binding force of the limiting interpretation of "storage device" recorded in the patent examination file for interpreting the claims of this patent on the grounds that the amendment to "storage device" was voluntary. 4. According to the legislative intent of Article 33 of the Patent Law, the invalidation caused by amendments exceeding the scope of the original disclosure should be limited to the part of the amendment that exceeds the original scope, and should not lead to the invalidation of the original technical solution that did not exceed the original scope. In this case, when, under the legal and correct claim interpretation method, "storage device" in this patent could be interpreted as "semiconductor storage device," which did not exceed the scope of the original disclosure, Decision No. 11291 interpreted "storage device" as various storage devices exceeding the original scope and thereby declared the entire patent invalid. This practice completely deviated from the legislative intent of Article 33 of the Patent Law.

The Patent Reexamination Board stated its opinion, arguing that the judgment of second instance was unclear in the finding of facts and improper in the application of law and should be revoked, and that Decision No. 11291 of the Patent Reexamination Board should be upheld. The main reasons were: 1. The judgment of second instance was erroneous in finding the meanings of "semiconductor storage device" and "storage device." According to the evidence submitted by the Patent Reexamination Board, storage devices included semiconductor memory, magnetic core memory, photoelectric memory, etc. Based on the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art, "semiconductor storage device" and "storage device" had different meanings; "semiconductor storage device" was only one type of "storage device." The original publication of this patent used "semiconductor storage device" throughout the description of the technical solution, and the term "storage device" appeared only twice in the "background art" section. (1) Regarding the first occurrence of "storage device," considering the internal logic of the background art section as a whole, it precisely demonstrated that this patent was directed only to "semiconductor storage devices." The background art of the original publication started from the technical problem that print head resolution and ink characteristics affect print quality in inkjet printing devices, proposing the technical concept of providing a storage device. However, the storage device had to be replaced, so Japanese Patent No. 2594912 proposed the technical concept of using a semiconductor storage device and electrodes on the printing device body. This patent application was precisely directed to the technical problem of poor contact and data loss in the inkjet printing device disclosed in Japanese Patent No. 2594912, which provided a semiconductor storage device on the ink cartridge and a set of electrodes on the printing device. It proposed installing a circuit board on the side wall of the ink cartridge, with contacts on the outside of the circuit board that could connect to an external control device, thereby achieving the technical effect that the external control device could access the semiconductor storage device through the contacts. Therefore, the technical solution of this patent was directed to printing devices and ink cartridges with semiconductor storage devices. The judgment of second instance, disregarding the part of the original publication related to the prior Japanese patent, found that this patent used "storage device" in the sense of "semiconductor storage device," which was clearly inconsistent with the facts. (2) Regarding the second occurrence of "storage device," according to the PCT international publication of this patent application, it could be proven that it was a mistranslation of "semiconductor storage device." According to the PCT international publication, it should be understood as "providing a semiconductor storage device on an ink cartridge and an electrode connected to the semiconductor storage device." The "storage device" here referred to the earlier "semiconductor storage device." 2. The judgment of second instance misunderstood the legislative intent of Article 33 of the Patent Law. The purpose of this article was to safeguard the first-to-file principle. Given the existence of provisions distinguishing prior art based on the filing date, a patent applicant could not change the content of the technical solution described in the application documents after the filing date was determined. Amendments to patent application documents could be classified as voluntary or involuntary based on timing, and as clarifying or adjusting based on content. Involuntary amendments could be clarifying or adjusting, while voluntary amendments were only adjusting. For adjusting amendments, it was necessary to consider estoppel in conjunction with the timing and content of the amendment, to avoid the parties "benefiting from both sides" through interpretation of the scope of claim protection, which would harm the public notice function of the patent. Regarding the amendments in this patent application, the patent applicant changed "semiconductor storage device" in the original application to "storage device" in a voluntary amendment when filing the divisional application, not a clarifying amendment in response to an examiner's requirement during substantive examination. The first office action in the substantive examination did not address "semiconductor storage device." Moreover, the technical solution containing the "semiconductor storage device" feature had already been granted in the original application. The patent applicant's voluntary amendment from "semiconductor storage device" to "storage device" indicated that they considered the two terms to have different meanings; otherwise, the amendment would have been meaningless. However, the patentee then argued in the invalidation proceedings that the scope of protection of "semiconductor storage device" and "storage device" was the same. This showed that the amendment process reflected estoppel, and it should be determined that changing "semiconductor storage device" to "storage device" constituted estoppel. Under these circumstances, it should not be found to comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law through claim interpretation. 3. The judgment of second instance was erroneous in both the timing and method of interpreting the scope of claim protection. (1) Regarding the timing of interpreting the scope of claim protection. As a legal document determining the scope of patent protection, the claims should, as much as possible, without relying on other documents, clearly and definitely define the scope of protection based on their own wording. To protect the public notice function of the patent, interpretation of the scope of claim protection should generally not be undertaken. Interpretation was only appropriate when the terms in the claims had specific meanings clearly defined in the specification, the specification clearly disclaimed certain technical solutions, some technical solutions included in the claims could not be realized, or the terms in the claims had multiple meanings. In this case, "storage device" had a clear meaning for a person of ordinary skill in the art and was not specifically defined in the specification. Under these circumstances, the interpretation of the claims in the judgment of second instance did not meet the timing requirement for interpreting the scope of claim protection. (2) Regarding the method of interpreting the scope of claim protection. Referring to Article 3 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Patent Infringement Dispute Cases, for interpreting the scope of claim protection, internal evidence such as the description, drawings, relevant claims, and the patent examination file had relatively higher priority as bases for claim interpretation. Regarding the parties' statements and the common understanding in the art, when the specification did not provide a clear definition, the common understanding in the art needed to be considered as a priority factor. Considering the two basic value orientations involved in interpreting the scope of claim protection, this view aimed to safeguard the public notice function of the patent while also protecting the legitimate interests of the patentee. If, based on a party's statement not recorded in the specification, the scope of claim protection was interpreted differently from the common understanding in the art, it would clearly harm the public notice function of the patent. In this case, the wording in the specification distinguished between "storage device" and "semiconductor storage device." Combined with the circumstances of the parent application from which this divisional application derived and the voluntary amendment by the patent applicant, it should objectively be determined that "storage device" and "semiconductor storage device" had different meanings. The judgment of second instance interpreted "storage device" as an abbreviation for "semiconductor storage device." This interpretation had no basis in the specification and differed from the general understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art, clearly harming the public notice function of the patent and depriving the public of predictability regarding the scope of patent protection.

The Court finds upon review that the facts found by the court of first instance are substantially true. Seiko Epson filed a divisional application for Invention Patent Application No. 99800780.3 and submitted amended documents on December 26, 2000 and January 28, 2002 respectively. In the claims submitted on January 28, 2002, the term "semiconductor storage device" no longer appeared, while the term "storage device" or "the storage device" appeared in Claims 19, 21, 36, 37, and 38 of that set of claims. On November 8, 2002, the State Intellectual Property Office issued a first Office Action to Seiko Epson regarding the description (pages 1-10) submitted on December 26, 2000, the claims (pages 1-7) submitted on January 28, 2002, and the abstract and abstract drawing submitted on the filing date. The body of the Office Action stated that part of the newly submitted claims exceeded the scope of the original description and claims, and did not comply with the provisions of Article 33 of the Patent Law. However, the Office Action did not address the issue of whether the amendment regarding "storage device" complied with Article 33 of the Patent Law. On May 9, 2003, Seiko Epson submitted an opinion statement in response to the first Office Action, amending the original claims by modifying original claim 23 into new claim 1.
